**Counts of reports with at least one recommendation mentioning "suicide"** (data as of 2026-11-04, not stale):

| Year published | Reports | Matching recommendations |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 | 56 | 98 |
| 2025 | 11 | 19 |

**On this evidence, suicide prevention is not growing as an OIG theme. The count fell sharply, from 56 reports to 11.** The numbers can't tell you why, so I wouldn't read the drop as a real decline in attention either.

**What the counts can show**
- They show how many published reports have a recommendation whose text contains the word "suicide", in each year.
- They show how many recommendations those reports contain, which is 98 in 2024 and 19 in 2025.

**What they cannot show**
- **Why the count changed.** A fall could mean OIG shifted its attention, the inspection protocols changed, or fewer reports were published. It could also mean the problem improved, though this data doesn't support that reading.
- **Whether 2025 is complete.** The 2025 recommendations are newer. Reports published late in the year may have had less time to appear in the data, and 6 of the 19 are still open. Also, some reports have no recommendations, and the counts leave those out.
- **Share of all reports.** I didn't pull the total number of reports or recommendations for each year. Without that, I can't say whether suicide's share of OIG's work rose or fell, as opposed to the raw count.
- **The full theme.** A keyword match on recommendation text misses reports that cover suicide prevention without using the word in a recommendation. It also catches reports where "suicide" is only mentioned in passing. OIG's "Suicide Prevention" topic tag covers only about a quarter of reports, so I didn't use it as a substitute.
- **Severity or quality.** The counts say nothing about how serious the findings were or how VA responded.

I can run the same count against total recommendations per year to get a share, or split it by report type, such as inspections versus hotline reviews. Either would show whether the change comes from the inspection program or from something else.

**The median for VBA recommendations is 179 days.** The middle half of them close between 134 days (Q1) and 312.5 days (Q3). The data is as of 2026-11-04 and is not stale.

**What it measures:** The days run from the report's publication to the closure date shown on OIG's site. That date appears to be when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing evidence. It can come months after the VBA actually finished the work, so the figure is probably longer than the real time to fix the problem.

**Details:**
- VBA has 966 recommendations. Of these, 923 are closed (897 implemented and 26 not implemented, a 2.8% rate) and 43 are open.
- The median uses 914 recommendations. The rest have no closure date on OIG's site, which is mostly the case for items from 2013 to 2016.
- 110 recommendations were closed on the day the report was published, presumably because the work was done beforehand. They are included in the median and pull it down.
- The 43 open items have a median age of 161 days. 17 are more than a year old, and the oldest is 1,567 days old.
- Only 7 recommendations have a target date, so this data can't show whether VBA met its deadlines. A target is the facility's own estimate, and a closure after it doesn't mean the deadline was missed.

Data as of 2026-11-04, and not stale. The data comes from VA OIG public reports.

## Next inspection window
- **Estimate only: around January 2028.** That is the latest inspection (ended 2025-01-16, report 25-00193-155) plus about three years. OIG publishes no schedule, so treat this as a planning assumption.
- Report 25-00193-155 shows a published date of 2026-07-16 in this dataset. I haven't checked that date against the inspection end date.

## Your open recommendations (4)
| Rec | Report | Finding | Target date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system) | Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment (Environment of Care). | 2027-01-29 |
| 2 | 25-00193-155 | The Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days (Primary Care). | 2026-12-31 |
| 5 | [23-01179-204](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare) | Ensure a video surveillance system is operational and monitored for the data center (OIT). | None listed |
| 7 | 23-01179-204 | Ensure water detection sensors are implemented in the data center (OIT). | None listed |

**What your responses commit you to:**
- **Cleanliness (rec 1):**
  - Restroom cleaning logs and signage.
  - A designated EMS tech who inspects high-traffic restrooms.
  - 24 new cleaning SOPs, with staff trained on June 2, 2026.
  - Daily oversight by the Chief of EMS.
  - Weekly Associate Director EOC rounds.
  - Have evidence ready that these are happening, such as completed logs and rounds records.
- **Toxic exposure screening (rec 2):**
  - Zero secondary screens were overdue as of June 1, 2026.
  - The SOP to formalize the process was still under development when you responded. Finalize it.
  - Monthly reporting to the Clinical Executive Council began June 2026.
  - The goal is six consecutive months at zero overdue. Counting from June, that point falls around November–December 2026, so confirm your actual run before the 2026-12-31 target.
- **Data center items (recs 5 and 7):** These two 2023 information security recommendations are still open and show no target date or facility response in this dataset. The action office is OIT, so check with your local OIT and ISO on status. Closure evidence may exist that this dataset doesn't capture.

## Repeat findings
None found. The check compares templated recommendations across your reports, and a repeat means the same issue was cited again.

## Common findings at peer facilities
These are ranked by how often they appear. They are not ranked by severity, and they don't predict what OIG will find at your facility. None of them is currently in your recommendation history.

1. **Communicating test results (clusters 260 and 261):** Workflows must show each team member's role under VHA Directive 1088(1).
   - Cluster 260 appears in 21 of 112 reports, and 17 are still open.
   - Cluster 261 appears in 12 of 112 reports. Its median time to close is about 256 days, based on a small sample of 9.
   - Peers committed to service-level workflow templates, Quality Management audits of each service's workflow, and monthly random chart reviews. Hampton's plan reviewed 50 results a month until 90% compliance held for six consecutive months. Examples: Middleton (25-00254-277), Shreveport (26-00057-170), Hampton (24-00603-86), Harlingen (25-00189-199).
2. **Clean environment (clusters 262 and 264):** Your own rec 1 is in this theme.
   - Cluster 262 appears in 11 of 112 reports, and all 11 are open.
   - Cluster 264 appears in 9 of 112 reports, with a median of about 191 days to close.
   - Peers used monthly EMS supervisor audits with 90% compliance for several consecutive months, reported to the CEOC. Examples: Salisbury (26-00030-213), Little Rock (25-00203-180), St. Louis (24-00600-136), Louisville (24-03205-235).
3. **Stable and consistent leadership (cluster 263):** This appears in 9 of 112 reports. The median time to close is about 237 days.

Median-days figures come from small samples. Same-day closures can pull a median down to 0.

## Suggested next steps
1. Build an evidence binder for recs 1 and 2: logs, audit results, CEC minutes, and the finalized SOP.
2. Run your own monthly EMS audits and report them to the CEOC. Peers used a 90% threshold.
3. Do a mock review of test-result communication. Check that you have a current local policy and service-level workflows aligned with Directive 1088(1), and sample charts for patient notification.
4. Confirm status with OIT on the data center video surveillance and water sensors.
5. Review the other 2025 findings in the report. The response text says OIG made no recommendation on several items because you fixed them. Those were clean and soiled storage, expired masks, the emergency alert reset, and a damaged floor. Keep them sustained, because they are easy to re-cite.

   - **Test results:** Services lacked workflows for communicating test results to patients under VHA Directive 1088. This includes defining what non-provider staff are responsible for.

   - **Closed items:** These covered the recovery coordinator, bed reporting, the Columbia suicide risk screen before discharge, suicide prevention training, and the safety inspection team.
   - **Open items:**
     - Access to the inpatient unit's communal room.
     - Tracking of involuntary commitment requirements, and documenting commitment status.
     - Documenting medication risk and benefit discussions.
     - Discharge instructions that are easy to understand and explain each medication.
     - Completing suicide safety plans, and addressing lethal means beyond firearms and opioids.

- **[21-00299-162](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-va-ny)** (May 2022): a comprehensive inspection with 8 recommendations.
- **[20-02968-170](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/hotline-healthcare-inspection/improper-feeding-community-living-center-patient-who-died-and)** (Jun 2021): improper feeding of a community living center patient who died, and an inadequate review of the patient's care. It made 7 recommendations.
- Older reports cover pressure ulcers (2017), sterile processing and reusable equipment in the operating room (2016), ambulette services (2016), Hurricane Sandy funds, and administrative investigations. The data shows 0 recommendations for the Sandy and investigation reports.

**Patterns:** The profile shows no repeat findings, meaning the same templated recommendation cited in more than one report. That reflects how the tool compares recommendations. It doesn't mean nothing recurred. Environment-of-care and community living center issues do appear in more than one report across the years.

I can't give you a reliable "missed target" percentage. The data doesn't measure that, and the tool advises against computing an on-time rate. The raw figures are below. They are from VA OIG data as of 2026-11-04, which is current.

**VHA recommendations (13,440 total)**
- 10,158 have a parsed target date.
- 616 were closed by the target date.
- 8,633 were closed after the target date.
- 145 are still open and past the target date.
- For those closed after the target, the median gap was 165 days.

If you ignored the caveats, 8,778 of 10,158 (about 86%) were closed after their target or are open past it. I don't recommend quoting that figure as a miss rate, for three reasons:
- **Targets are estimates.** A target date is the facility's own estimate, not a binding deadline.
- **Closure dates lag the work.** A closure date appears to record when OIG closed the item after reviewing evidence. That can come months after the work was finished.
- **Coverage is incomplete.** About 24% of VHA recommendations (3,282 of 13,440) have no parsed target date and aren't in the figures above.

A closure after the target date, or an open item past it, therefore doesn't show that a facility missed its commitment.

Other VHA figures that are measurable:
- The median time to closure is 225 days (middle half: 153 to 326 days).
- 426 recommendations are open. 108 of those have been open more than a year, and the oldest has been open 2,078 days.
- Only 36 closed recommendations (0.28%) were closed as not implemented.

The source is VA OIG's recommendations data at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all.

I can't name a worst VA medical center, because OIG doesn't rank or rate facilities that way. It publishes inspection reports and recommendations for each facility. It doesn't publish a single score or a "worst" list. Any ranking I gave you would be my own invention, not an OIG finding.

Raw counts of findings or recommendations would also mislead. They depend on how many inspections a facility has had, how large it is, and how thorough the inspection was. A facility with more recommendations may simply have been inspected more recently or more often. Some of those recommendations may also already be closed.

I can do any of these instead, using the OIG data:
- **Look up a specific facility.** I can pull its reports, open recommendations, and any repeat findings.
- **Show systemic issues.** I can find the findings that recur most often across many facilities, such as staffing, patient safety, or environment-of-care problems.
- **Compare a facility with its peers.** I can show how its findings stack up against similar facilities in the same VISN or state.
